title: Dining Table

altText: A long, narrow wooden dining table with a plain flat top, standing on simple legs.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, culture, date, medium, dimensions (about 27 1/2 x 122 1/4 x 33 1/4 in.), credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: An American dining table dated 1825–50 in the Met record, made of pine and birch. It is long and narrow, about 122 inches (310 cm) in length, or more than ten feet, which suggests it was made to seat many people at once. The record names no maker.

descriptions.k: This is a very long wooden table for eating. It is longer than a big couch. It is made of pine and birch wood. A lot of people could sit here. Who would you invite to dinner?
descriptions.g12: This table is more than ten feet long. That is longer than a big couch. It was made in America almost two hundred years ago from pine and birch wood. Many people could sit and eat here together. Look at its flat top and plain legs. Who do you think ate here?
descriptions.g35: This dining table was made in the United States between 1825 and 1850. It is more than ten feet long but only a little over two feet high and under three feet wide. Pine and birch are common woods, and the table is plain, with a long flat top. Who might have needed such a long table? What do its simple parts tell you about how it was used?
descriptions.g68: This American dining table, dated 1825–50 and made of pine and birch, is more than ten feet long, long enough to seat a large household or a workforce. Pine and birch were common, affordable woods. Its simple construction suggests practical use over display. What can an everyday table tell us about daily routines, work, and family life? How does its length shape the feeling of a shared meal?
descriptions.g910: This 1825–50 dining table prioritizes capacity and plainness over ornament. At more than ten feet long, it indicates communal dining at a scale larger than most single families, and the Met's listing of pine and birch points to affordable, locally available materials. Its form invites questions about who gathered here and how seating shaped social order. Consider how the absence of decoration can still communicate values of utility, community, and labor.
descriptions.g1112: A table more than ten feet long, built of pine and birch between 1825 and 1850, implies communal eating on a scale beyond a typical household. The Met record names no maker, so its history must be inferred from form, scale, and materials rather than documents. Plain furniture of this kind complicates narratives that emphasize luxury objects, and asks who is represented in museum collections of household goods. Ask how this table organizes social relationships, labor, and daily life, and where interpretation outruns the evidence.

teacherNote.context: Plain furniture of pine and birch was widely made in the early United States. The Met record dates this dining table to 1825–50 and gives its length as about 122 inches.
directions: Have students mark out 122 inches on the classroom floor and discuss who and what could fit along it.
Ask students to compare this table with a fancy table in the archive and say what each tells about its users.
Discuss how everyday objects without a known maker can still teach us about the past.
